entry.title: Supabase Under the Hood: What Actually Happens When You Listen to Postgres Changes
entry.summary: When you call supabase.channel('room-1').on('postgres_changes', ...) in your client application, it feels simple. A row updates in your database, and your frontend state updates a few milliseconds later. Most developers assume Supabase runs a basic WebSocket server that connects to PostgreSQL, sets up an event listener, and forwards JSON payloads. Some assume it relies on PostgreSQL's built-in LISTEN and NOTIFY commands. Neither assumption is correct. Underneath that client method is an infrastructure pipeline involving PostgreSQL Write-Ahead Logs (WAL), binary logical decoding plugins, an Elixir clustering engine, and an in-database row evaluation system called WALRUS. entry.title: Data Cleanup Across Multiple Worker Nodes: Node.js 3-Worker Lease Explained
entry.summary:
A renewal reminder in an education product should wait for the business deadline, then run once. The least complex design that holds up across three worker nodes is a durable work table plus a lease: claim a row atomically, process a small batch, and let an expired lease return the row to the pool. The lease is the boundary. That choice gives a solo SaaS team a useful balance. A queue can improve wake-up latency, but it adds delivery semantics and another operational surface. A database poller costs a few seconds of latency in exchange for fewer moving parts. For a reminder that is due at 09:00 on a school administrator's renewal date, that trade usually favors the poller unless the product has a strict sub-second requirement.

entry.title: How to get honest feedback on your app before you launch
entry.summary: You built the app. Your friends say it looks great. That tells you nothing. Here is the checklist I use now. I run TestMyBuild, a site where builders get feedback from real testers, so I read feedback posts every day. These are the things that decide whether you get something useful back. "What do you think?" gets you "looks nice". Ask one question a stranger can answer in five minutes. Could you sign up without help? Did you understand what the app does before you scrolled? Where did you stop? A tester gives you a few minutes. If the app needs a credit card, a waitlist or an invite code, they are gone. Make it free or give a free trial. If sign-up is heavy, offer a test account. Tell people what is finished and what is not. Otherwise half the feedback is about the thing you already know is broken. Places where asking is normal: the Show HN section of Hacker News, the feedback threads on Indie Hackers, the app announcement forums for your platform, and subreddits that have a weekly feedback thread. Read the rules first. Give feedback to two other people before you ask for your own. "The button did not work" is hard to fix. The same sentence with a screenshot takes one minute. Always ask for one. Thank them, say what you will change, and say what you will not change and why. The next tester reads those replies and decides whether you are worth the effort. One person hating your onboarding is an opinion. Three people stopping at the same screen is a bug. Wait for the pattern, then fix the top one and ask again. The cheapest way to get testers is to be one. Test someone's app properly and most builders return it. That last point is how TestMyBuild works: you earn the credits for your own listing by testing other people's apps, and a person on our team tests every app first, so nobody gets silence. It is at testmybuild.app if you want it. The checklist works without it too.
